notes.h: What a code of ethics is
notes.b: Every sport needs shared rules about how people behave, not just rules about how the game is played. A code of ethics writes those expectations down so that everyone knows them.
points: A code of ethics is a written set of principles and standards of behaviour expected of everyone involved in a sport, including players, coaches, parents, spectators and officials.
It is usually published by the sport's national governing body (the organisation that runs the sport across the country) or by a club.
A code of conduct is the more detailed part: it sets out the specific behaviours expected of each group involved in the sport, so each person knows exactly what is asked of them.
notes.tip: If asked what a code of ethics is, give the written principles and standards of behaviour for everyone involved. If asked how it applies, pick one group (participant, parent, spectator, coach or club official) and give its specific behaviours.

notes.h: Why sports have codes of ethics
notes.b: A code is not paperwork for its own sake. Each reason below answers a real problem that sport faces when people behave badly.
points: They protect participants, especially children, because young people are the most vulnerable to poor treatment in sport.
They promote fair play (playing honestly within the rules) and respect between everyone involved.
They set clear standards of behaviour for everyone involved, so nobody can claim they did not know what was expected.
They give the club or governing body a basis for discipline, because a person who breaks the written code can be dealt with against a standard that was agreed in advance.
They protect the sport's image, because a sport known for abuse or cheating loses members, volunteers and public respect.

notes.b: In Ireland the protection of children in sport is organised at three levels: a national code, the governing bodies of each sport, and the individual club.
points: Sport Ireland publishes the Code of Ethics and Good Practice for Children's Sport, which is child-centred (it puts the child's needs first) and promotes safe sport.
National governing bodies adopt codes of conduct and child safeguarding policies (the rules and procedures that keep children safe from harm) for their own sport.
Clubs appoint a children's officer or a designated liaison person for child safeguarding, so that there is a named person in the club who deals with child safeguarding concerns.

notes.b: Participants are the players themselves. Their code is about how they treat the game, the people they play against and the people who run it.
points: Play by the rules and within the spirit of the game, which means respecting what the rules are trying to achieve, not just their wording.
Respect opponents and officials (referees, umpires and other match officials), because the game cannot happen without them.
Never cheat, never dope (use banned performance-enhancing substances) and never abuse anyone.
Do your best and be a good team-mate.
notes.tip: For a participant code, include no cheating or doping, no abuse, respect for opponents and officials, doing your best and being a good team-mate.

notes.b: Parents are not on the pitch, but their behaviour shapes how a child experiences sport. Their code is about supporting the child without adding pressure.
points: Encourage the child rather than pressure them, because pressure from a parent can take the fun out of playing.
Focus on enjoyment and effort rather than only the result, so the child learns that trying matters as well as winning.
Respect the decisions of coaches and officials, even when disagreeing with them.
Model good behaviour on the sideline, because children copy how the adults around them behave.
Support the club.

notes.b: Spectators watch rather than play, but their noise and behaviour affect players and officials directly. Their code is short and about respect.
points: Applaud good play by both sides, not only by the team you support.
Never abuse players or officials.
Respect the venue and its rules.

notes.b: Coaches have power over players and are role models for them. Their code is the longest because their influence is the greatest.
points: Put the welfare of players first, ahead of winning.
Treat all players fairly.
Be qualified and trained in child safeguarding (protecting children from harm), because coaches spend time with young players.
Model fair play in their own conduct, so players see the behaviour they are asked to copy.
Never encourage cheating or doping.
Use positive coaching, praising effort and correct behaviour.

notes.b: Club officials (the committee members and others who run the club) are responsible for the whole organisation. Their code covers how the club is run and how problems are handled.
points: Run the club fairly and transparently, meaning decisions are made openly and not in secret.
Implement child safeguarding policies, so the written rules are actually put into practice.
Ensure coaches are qualified and facilities are safe, because the club is responsible for the people and places its members use.
Deal with complaints and discipline consistently, so that everyone is treated by the same standard.

notes.b: An exam may ask you to write statements for a code. Each one has to turn a principle into a clear instruction for a particular group.
points: Each statement should comply with the principles of ethical practice, which are set out in the notes on principles of ethical practice.
Each statement should name who it applies to and what that person must do, so it is a clear instruction.
Example: Players will accept the referee's decision without dissent (open disagreement).
Example: Coaches will give every player a fair opportunity to take part.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to list statements that comply with the principles of ethical practice. Name the group and the behaviour in each, as in the two examples.

notes.b: A code lists what people must do. Sportsmanship is the attitude behind it: how a good sport behaves when the result is at stake.
points: Definition: playing within the rules and the spirit of the game, with respect, honesty and grace in winning and losing.
Example: helping a fallen opponent up, which shows respect even in competition.
Example: kicking the ball out of play when an opponent is injured, so that play stops and the player can be treated.
Example: shaking hands with opponents and applauding them at the end of a match, which shows grace whether you win or lose.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to explain sportsmanship and to tell which picture shows it. Define it, then give examples such as helping a fallen opponent or shaking hands.

notes.b: Gamesmanship sits in a grey area between fair play and cheating. The player stays inside the rules on paper but uses tactics that go against their spirit.
points: Definition: bending the rules, or using dubious, psychological or time-wasting tactics, to gain an advantage without technically cheating.
Gamesmanship is not outright cheating: doping, for example, is cheating rather than gamesmanship.
Time-wasting: deliberately delaying a restart of play, for instance to run down the clock when ahead.
Feigning injury (pretending to be hurt), or diving to win a free (falling over on purpose to get a free kick or free).
Psychological tactics: sledging an opponent (insulting or taunting them to put them off), or unsettling them before a serve.
notes.tip: Do not call doping gamesmanship: it is cheating. Give several different examples, because a question can say you cannot use faking injury. Exams ask you to define gamesmanship and give two examples.

notes.h: How sportsmanship and gamesmanship affect engagement
notes.b: Engagement means people taking part and staying involved in a sport, as players, volunteers or officials. The way people behave decides whether they stay.
points: Sportsmanship creates a positive, safe and enjoyable environment that keeps people involved.
Sportsmanship attracts new participants and volunteers, because people want to join a club that treats its members well.
Gamesmanship can sour the experience and cause conflict between players, teams and officials.
Gamesmanship can lead to drop-out, especially of young players and officials, who may decide the sport is not worth the stress.
Gamesmanship can damage the sport's image.
Gamesmanship may win in the short term, but it erodes engagement over time.
notes.tip: To describe the impact of sportsmanship or gamesmanship on engagement, give two examples, such as new participants attracted or young players and officials dropping out. Exams also ask you to discuss the difference between the two.

keyTerms.definition: A written set of principles and standards of behaviour expected of everyone involved in a sport.
A set of specific behaviours expected of each group involved in a sport.
The body that governs a sport at national level and usually publishes its codes.
Policies and practices that protect children from abuse, neglect and harm in sport.

keyTerms.term: Code of Ethics and Good Practice for Children's Sport
keyTerms.definition: The code published by Sport Ireland that promotes child-centred, safe sport.
A club official appointed to look after the welfare of children.
Playing within the rules and the spirit of the game, with respect, honesty and grace in winning and losing.
Bending the rules or using dubious tactics to gain an advantage without technically cheating.
Taking part in physical activity and sport and staying involved in it.
Coaching that rewards effort and good behaviour rather than only results.

factCards.definition: The Code of Ethics and Good Practice for Children's Sport: child-centred and promoting safe sport.
Helping a fallen opponent up, or kicking the ball out of play when an opponent is injured.
Time-wasting, feigning injury, diving to win a free, sledging, deliberately delaying a restart, unsettling an opponent before a serve.
It sours the experience, causes conflict, drives out young players and officials, and damages the sport's image.

questions.prompt: Describe, using two examples, the impact of gamesmanship on engagement in physical activity.
questions.model: Gamesmanship damages engagement in two main ways. First, feigning injury or diving to win a free makes a match feel unfair and disrupts its flow, frustrating opponents and spectators, and it can push people away from the sport. Second, sledging or unsettling an opponent before a serve creates conflict and hostility; young players and officials, in particular, may drop out rather than face it, which shrinks the number of participants and volunteers. Gamesmanship may win a contest in the short term, but over time it erodes engagement and damages the sport's image.

questions.prompt: List four statements that comply with the principles of ethical practice and could be included in a code of ethics for sport.
questions.model: 1. Players will accept the referee's decision without dissent. 2. Coaches will give every player a fair opportunity to take part. 3. Spectators will applaud good play by both teams and will not abuse players or officials. 4. Club officials will give every member access to coaching and facilities according to their needs.

questions.prompt: Explain sportsmanship and give an example of it in a physical activity of your choice.
questions.model: Sportsmanship means playing within the rules and the spirit of the game, with respect, honesty and grace in winning and losing. Example in soccer: a player kicks the ball out of play when an opponent is injured, so that play stops and the injured player can be treated, and then applauds that opponent at the end of the match.
